items: Building a site no longer freezes Graft. On PCs where Windows Security’s Controlled folder access protects Documents, Windows blocked the new site’s folder and Graft waited forever. New sites now go in a Graft Sites folder in your user folder, which Windows doesn’t lock and OneDrive doesn’t sync; sites already in Documents › Graft Sites stay there.
When Windows won’t let Graft create or change a file, Graft and the agent now say so and how to allow it, instead of hanging or reporting “no such file or directory”.

Sites: describe a website and Graft designs and builds it, then hosts it on your computer at its own address (like peach-palace.localhost) with a live preview that reloads as it changes. The Sites tab keeps a gallery of them with previews, and each is a folder in Documents › Graft Sites, ready to publish anywhere.

Connected apps work properly: Roblox Studio tools that appear after it connects now show up, servers that start empty are asked again, long jobs that report progress (a render, a download) are no longer cut off after two minutes, apps started with npx or uvx get your full environment, older HTTP servers work, and a server that crashes reconnects. When Blender, Roblox Studio or Unity isn’t ready, Graft says what to check.
Chats can use your connected apps too, asking before each action.
Taproot grows a root: picking the deepest effort turns the slider into a living leaf-to-gold gradient, draws a small root and says what it costs.

Computer use is easier to follow: a ring marks each click, the banner says what the agent is doing, each step shows its screenshot in the chat, and the agent can zoom in to read small text or open an app by name.
Fixes: a moved or deleted project folder no longer shows as “Git is not installed”, Git is found even when it isn’t on PATH, and session titles work for people using free models with no credits.

Checks after changes: list your project’s checks (type check, lint, tests) in Customize → Checks and Graft runs them after every turn that changed files. When one fails, the agent gets the output and fixes the cause, up to two rounds. Graft suggests the commands from your package.json, Cargo, Go or Python setup.

A sandbox for code you don’t trust: turn it on for a project and its commands run in a Docker or Podman container that sees only the project folder. Your other files, keys, credentials and environment variables stay out of reach, .git and .graft are read-only inside it, and one switch cuts off the network. In Auto-edit and Auto, sandboxed commands run without asking.

A better Browser panel: a console with an error badge, find in page, zoom, phone and tablet widths, developer tools, reload without cache and clearing site data. Send a screenshot, a picked element or the console straight into your message. With no page open it lists the dev servers running on your computer.
The agent can test web apps: it opens your dev server in the Browser panel, clicks and types like a person, reads the console and takes screenshots.
Fixes: Stop now clears a waiting approval or question, the changes panel works for sessions in a subfolder of a repository, and a session list that fails to load offers a retry.

Integrations: connect Blender, Roblox Studio, Unity, Godot, Figma, a Playwright browser, GitHub, Context7, Sentry, Linear and Notion from Settings → Integrations. Graft checks what each one needs on your computer, shows the setup steps and adds it in one click.
Tokens you give an integration are kept encrypted with your system keyring, not in a settings file.
The command palette matches what you type more precisely: letters scattered across a long command no longer count as a match.
Long tasks no longer stop at 150 steps: a turn runs until the work is done. You can still set a limit in Settings → Permissions, and a turn that reaches it pauses with a Continue button.
A command palette: press Ctrl+Shift+P, or type > in search, to run almost anything. Start sessions, switch palettes and themes, open any settings page, export, compact or rewind.

Settings → Personalization tells Graft about you and how you like answers, with a response style (balanced, concise, explanatory or learning) and your own instructions. Chats and code sessions use it; incognito chats never do.
Rewritten instructions for chats and code sessions, and View system prompt (session menu or /system) shows exactly what Graft sends to the model.
Six colour palettes, each light and dark (Graft, Midnight, Slate, Grove, Dune and High contrast), seven accent colours, and smoother motion throughout.
Start a message with ! in a code session to run a shell command yourself, such as !npm test; Graft sees the output with your next message. ↑ and ↓ bring back messages you sent.
Custom agents: make specialists such as a reviewer, a test writer or a debugger in Customize → Agents, and Graft hands them tasks.
New commands: /commit, /pr, /security-review, /explain, /test, /export, /system and /new. A command file of your own can replace any of the prompt commands.
Messages you type while Graft works can go right away: Send now hands one over after the current step without stopping anything. Queued messages can also be edited or removed, in chats too.
Scion the sprout comes alive: it blinks, looks around and wiggles its leaves, flaps them while Graft works, and hops when you hover over it or click it.

Updates work again. Every earlier version failed its update check (“Cannot set properties of undefined”), so install this one by hand once; from here on Graft downloads new versions itself and asks to restart.
If an update check ever fails, Settings → About links straight to the releases page so you can download the newest installer yourself.
A copy of Graft that can’t update itself now says so instead of showing “Checking for updates…” forever.
Chats can make files for you to download (documents, data, code, pictures) and run JavaScript in a locked-down sandbox for calculations and data work.
Chats know the time: each message carries when it was sent, so “what time is it?” gets a real answer.

Read aloud can pause, resume and stop, and sounds far more natural with OpenRouter’s voices (Kokoro by default, about $0.0006 per 1,000 characters). Pick the voice and speed in Settings → Voice; incognito chats always use your computer’s voice.
Taproot answers questions and quick requests directly instead of planning and reviewing work that never happened.
Free web search with no key or account: Exa by default, and DuckDuckGo when Exa is busy. Searching no longer costs anything unless you pick a paid engine.
The engine you pick in Settings → Web search now decides every search; Claude’s built-in search runs only when you pick Anthropic.
Site icons load for far more sites, YouTube and npm among them, and a site without one shows a globe instead of a letter.
On Windows, the taskbar shows Graft’s own icon and name instead of Electron’s.
Web search in chats and code sessions through your own provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini or OpenRouter), or Brave, Tavily or SearXNG, with site chips while it searches and cited sources as pills.
Each turn’s work folds into one line with a live status while it runs, and an “Edited N files” card lists every change with its diff.
Taproot now investigates, plans with a task list it has to finish, verifies with real checks and reviews its own diff before reporting.
Computer use on Windows (opt-in in Settings → Permissions): the agent can see the screen and use the mouse and keyboard, asking first, and Ctrl+Alt+Esc stops it.
Updates from GitHub releases, with a prompt to restart when one is ready; a transcript width setting; faster startup.
Checkpoints and rewind work with older Git versions too, including the one macOS ships, and Linux builds come as an AppImage and a .deb.
Meet Scion: the pixel sprout is now Graft’s icon in the taskbar, the tray and the installer, and its mark inside the app.
Over 200 providers from an open model catalog, with a searchable picker, per-model effort levels and accurate costs.
Settings → Privacy: ask providers not to train on your data, and incognito chats that stay off your computer.
A real Bypass mode you switch on in Settings, plus Files and “Keep computer awake” in the session menu.
Prompt caching for Claude models on OpenRouter, and session spend in the context popover.
Code sessions with a real agent loop: read, edit, search, run commands and fetch pages, with a permission prompt for anything risky.
Five permission modes, including Plan (read-only until you approve a plan) and Auto (low-risk actions run without asking).
Git worktrees per session, hidden checkpoints before every turn, and rewind for files, conversation or both.
Works with Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, OpenRouter, Ollama and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
Taproot: a long-horizon effort mode that keeps going until the work is verified.
